# Building 4410: Division 26 project specifications (final submittal)

You are the electrical Designer of Record at Harlan Sato Engineers LLC, the architect-engineer for the new Company
Operations Facility, Building 4410, at Fort Calder, an Army design-bid-build project. The electrical design is
complete and coordinated in a building information model. Your task order is to produce the **Division 26 project
specifications** that tell the general contractor and the electrical contractor what to buy and how to install and
test it, edited from the Unified Facilities Guide Specifications to this project's criteria, owner requirements and
installation standard, together with the electrical design basis the specifications rest on.

The project documents are in this workspace: the A/E scope of work and design directives, the transmittal log and
design review comments, the Owner's Project Requirements, the installation electrical design standard, the drawings
and schedules, the electrical coordination model, the utility service data, the calculation basis memoranda, product
data and photometric files, the governing criteria and federal regulations, and the guide specification library. Some
folders hold superseded revisions or material from other agencies; the scope of work and the transmittal log say what
is current and what governs. The NFPA 70 text is not provided.

## What to deliver

`output/submission.zip` containing:

1. `specs/`: **one `.docx` per Division 26 section this task order delivers**, numbered and titled as the
   corresponding Unified Facilities Guide Specification, each a finished project section tailored from that guide
   specification. Edit the guide specification rather than writing sections from scratch: a document that does not
   retain the guide specification's text is not treated as a project section. The scope of work says which sections
   this task order delivers; sections delivered under another task order are neither required nor penalised.
2. `design_basis.xlsx`: the electrical design basis workbook, with these sheets (header in row 1, one record per
   row; extra columns are ignored):

| sheet | columns |
|---|---|
| `Sections` | `number`, `title`, `basis` (why the section is in the project) |
| `Feeders` | `feeder`, `route_length_ft`, `sets`, `size`, `raceway_in`, `vd_pct`, `fill_pct`: one row per feeder and service run on the one-line diagram |
| `ShortCircuit` | `bus`, `voltage_v`, `available_fault_ka`, `specified_rating_ka`: one row per switchboard, panelboard and transfer switch bus on the one-line diagram |
| `Photometric` | `space`, `luminaire_type`, `quantity`, `avg_maintained_fc`, `min_fc`, `uniformity`, `lpd_w_ft2`: one row per interior space in the coordination model |
| `StepLoad` | `step`, `loads`, `step_kva_start`, `voltage_dip_pct`, `recovery_s`: one row per load step, in the order the loads are placed on the engine-generator |
| `Register` | `req_id`, `document` (number/title, with revision or change where there are several), `clause` (paragraph, table, note or row), `requirement`, `value` (the governing number or choice), `applies_to` (section numbers) |
| `Findings` | `finding_id`, `document`, `location`, `defect`, `correction`: errors or inconsistencies you found in the furnished documents and how you resolved them |

## Section format

Each section document must read, as plain paragraphs of text:

- `SECTION nn nn nn` (the section number), the section title, and the section date line;
- `PART 1   GENERAL`, `PART 2   PRODUCTS`, `PART 3   EXECUTION` (a part without content reads `Not used.`);
- articles numbered as typed text, `1.1 REFERENCES`, `1.2 ...`, with upper-case titles; lower-level paragraphs
  `1.2.1 Title`; list items `a.`, `(1)`, `(a)`, `1.`;
- `-- End of Section --` as the last paragraph.

Numbering, list markers and section headings must be literal text in the paragraphs; automatic Word list numbering is
not read. Only paragraph text is read (tables in a section are read cell by cell as paragraphs). Any tool that writes a
valid `.docx` (WordprocessingML package) is fine; no word processor is installed in this workspace, and a `.docx` can be
written with the Python standard library (`zipfile` plus the three required parts: `[Content_Types].xml`, `_rels/.rels`,
`word/document.xml`). No BIM or photometric toolkit is installed either; the coordination model and the photometric
files are text formats and can be parsed with the standard library.

## How the package is judged

Each delivered section is judged as one item against requirements recomputed from the project documents,
independently of wording; values are compared after unit conversion. The design-basis sheets are judged by re-running
the calculations against the design you declare, and the numbers you report are checked against that re-run. A section
with an unresolved choice, or whose design is unsafe or unbuildable, fails a hard requirement family.
Specifications are performance-based and must not be more restrictive than the governing requirement
(FAR 11.002(a)(1)(ii)); a design that meets every limit without over-providing earns the most objective credit. A hard
governing requirement that a section's design rests on and that is missing from your `Register` fails one more hard
family of that section. Each section scores `0.4·p² + 0.6·h⁴·O`, where `p` is the weighted fraction of the section's
requirement families passed, `h` the weighted fraction of its hard families passed, and `O` its over-specification
credit, computed for every section: a failed hard family discounts `O` through `h⁴` instead of zeroing it.
There is no required number of rows on the `Register` and `Findings` sheets. Defects in the furnished documents and in
the furnished design are scored, so a defect you find and correct belongs on `Findings`, with the correction you made.


## Verifier access (blind variant)

No verifier, oracle, or evaluation data of any kind is available in this workspace; the
only checks you can run are the ones you build yourself. Work from the brief and the
documents alone and submit your best final deliverable; it will be graded offline by the
frozen verifier on held-out instances.

'Heading 1' Architect-Engineer Scope of Work — Electrical Design, Final (100 %) Submittal
'Normal' Contract W912XX-27-C-0418 (PN 90417). Company Operations Facility (COF), Building 4410, Fort Calder, Georgia. U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, Savannah District (fictional project).
'Heading 2' 1 GENERAL
'Normal' 1.1 Project. New two-story Company Operations Facility for an Army unit (Army project, new construction; no renovation). The facility is on an inland installation in Georgia; no state or local electrical amendments apply on the installation.
'Normal' 1.2 Delivery method. Design-bid-build. The A/E is the Designer of Record (DOR) and prepares the construction contract documents: drawings, specifications and the design analysis.
'Normal' 1.3 Scope of this task order. Prepare the Division 26 project specification sections listed in 3.9, and the electrical design basis workbook, for the final (100 %) submittal.
'Normal' Table 1 — Electrical systems inventory (1.3). Present: main switchboard MSB; 480 V panelboards HM1, H1A, H2A, HE1; dry-type transformers T-1A, T-2A, T-C1, T-E1; 208 V panelboards LP1A, LP2A, LC1, LE1; engine-generator GEN-1; automatic transfer switches ATS-L (Article 700, bypass-isolation) and ATS-E (Article 702); advanced meter; SPDs at MSB and LC1; grounding electrode system with ground ring; lightning protection system; interior and exterior LED lighting; variable frequency drives on AHU-1 and AHU-2 (furnished under Division 23). Not in this project: busway; power cable tray; motor control centers; lighting control panelboards / relay panels; residential load centers; hazardous (classified) locations; 400 Hz systems; 270 V dc systems; medium-voltage work (utility furnishes primary); UPS (owner-furnished rack units only); photovoltaic system; paralleling switchgear; fire pump. Water service: HDPE (nonmetallic). Service entrance: underground, six 4 in PVC Schedule 40 ducts, concrete-encased, from the utility pad-mounted transformer to MSB; the secondary service conductors are sized by the Designer of Record in the design basis (3.4), and the conductors shown on E-601 Rev C are the 35 % submittal selection.
'Normal' 1.3.1 Government-furnished electrical coordination model. The Government furnishes, with the contract drawings, the electrical coordination model 50_bim/BLDG4410-E_RevC.ifc, an IFC4 (ISO 16739-1) model of the building authored in millimetres. The model is a contract document. It carries the building spaces and their dimensions, the electrical equipment locations, the interior luminaires of each space, and the routed feeder raceways, each raceway run identified by the feeder tag it carries. Dimensions, luminaire quantities and locations, routed feeder lengths and raceway trade sizes are taken from the model: they are not dimensioned or scheduled on the drawings. Also furnished are the LM-63 photometric files of the scheduled interior luminaire types, in 40_product_data/photometrics.
'Normal' 1.4 Schedule. Construction award April 2027; electrical equipment deliveries (switchboard, dry-type transformers, generator, transfer switch) June 2028; beneficial occupancy March 2029.
'Normal' 1.5 Order of precedence. Where requirements of the following documents differ, the order of precedence is: (1) this SOW; (2) Unified Facilities Criteria and federal regulations; (3) the installation standard IES-26; (4) the Owner's Project Requirements (current revision). A lower-precedence document may add or tighten a requirement; the more stringent requirement then governs unless the higher-precedence document prohibits it. Superseded revisions have no standing. Use only the current revisions listed in the transmittal log.
'Heading 2' 2 CRITERIA
'Normal' 2.1 Design to UFC 1-200-01, UFC 3-501-01, UFC 3-520-01 (current change), the federal regulations in the criteria folder, IES-26 and the OPR. NFPA 70 (edition adopted by UFC 1-200-01) applies but is not furnished. UFC 1-200-02 high performance and sustainable building requirements apply; no third-party certification is sought.
'Normal' 2.2 Use the Unified Facilities Guide Specifications (UFGS) Division 26 masters furnished in the guide specification library (August 2026 update). Other agencies' master specifications in the library are for reference only and must not be used as project specification text.
'Heading 2' 3 SPECIFICATION REQUIREMENTS
'Normal' 3.1 Tailoring. Tailor each UFGS for an Army design-bid-build project: keep only the Army tailoring options, resolve every bracketed choice and blank, delete notes to the specifier, and delete requirements for equipment and systems the project does not have.
'Normal' 3.2 Photometrics. The DOR provides the photometric calculations in the design analysis; the specifications must not require the Contractor to prepare photometric plans.
'Normal' 3.3 Format. UFS 1-300-02 is incorporated into this SOW and is binding for the project specifications regardless of its For-Information-Only status. English (inch-pound) units only. Deliver each section as a separate DOCX document (the Government converts them to Google Docs for review).
'Normal' 3.4 Ratings and delegated design. The panelboard and switchboard schedules on the drawings do not show short-circuit current ratings: state the minimum short-circuit current rating of the switchboard and of the 480 V and 208 V panelboards in the specifications, from the short-circuit study basis SCB-01 method and the current utility data. Seismic restraint of electrical equipment is a Contractor delegated design by a registered professional engineer; the DOR reviews it.
'Normal' 3.5 Power system studies. The Contractor performs the short-circuit, protective device coordination and arc flash studies on as-built data in accordance with Section 26 05 73 and provides device settings; the DOR reviews them. Electronic-trip breakers are used to achieve selective coordination. The studies are construction-phase studies for protective device settings and arc flash labels; scope: from the utility transformer secondary through every 480 V and 208 V bus (MSB, HM1, H1A, H2A, ATS-E, HE1, ATS-L, LP1A, LP2A, LC1, LE1), for the normal and the generator source, using the utility data of UP-4410 Rev 2. The study engineer is a registered professional engineer with 5 years of power system study experience and seals the studies.
'Normal' 3.6 Submittal review. Classify submittals per UFS 1-300-02; every item requiring Government approval ('G') must carry the reviewer code of Table 2.
'Normal' 3.7 Operation and maintenance. Require O&M data per Section 01 78 23 and Army facility data per Section 01 78 24.00 10.
'Normal' 3.8 Cross-references. Cross-reference only sections in the project manual (Appendix A for other divisions, plus every Division 26 section of the project manual listed in 3.9), by number and exact title.
'Normal' 3.9 Division 26 sections delivered under this task order. Deliver, and only deliver, the following sections: 26 05 73 POWER SYSTEM STUDIES; 26 20 00 INTERIOR DISTRIBUTION SYSTEM; 26 24 13 SWITCHBOARDS; 26 32 15 ENGINE-GENERATOR SET, STATIONARY (STANDBY); 26 36 23 AUTOMATIC TRANSFER SWITCHES; 26 51 00 INTERIOR LIGHTING. The following Division 26 sections of the same project manual are delivered under Task Order 0003 by the same A/E and are not part of this submittal: 26 05 48 SEISMIC PROTECTION FOR ELECTRICAL EQUIPMENT; 26 08 00 APPARATUS INSPECTION AND TESTING; 26 41 00 LIGHTNING PROTECTION SYSTEM; 26 56 00 EXTERIOR LIGHTING. Those four sections are nevertheless part of the project manual, so cross-references to them from the sections delivered here remain valid and must be retained where the guide specification makes them. Nothing in this paragraph changes the scope of the facility: the building still has lightning protection, seismic restraint of electrical equipment, acceptance testing and exterior lighting, and the Owner's Project Requirements and IES-26 requirements for those systems continue to apply in full.
'Heading 2' 4 DELIVERABLES
'Normal' 4.1 One DOCX per Division 26 project specification section delivered under 3.9.
'Normal' 4.2 The electrical design basis workbook (design_basis.xlsx) with the section list, the short-circuit results used for the specified ratings, the requirements register and the findings on Government-furnished documents (including any finding against the coordination model). The workbook must also contain: (a) the feeder design — for every feeder, the routed length taken from the coordination model, the number of parallel sets, the conductor size, the calculated voltage drop, the calculated raceway fill and the allowable ampacity, by the method of FDB-01; (b) the photometric design — for every interior space, the luminaire type and quantity, the calculated average and minimum maintained illuminance, the calculated uniformity and the lighting power density, and the whole-building interior lighting power density, by the method of PCB-01; and (c) the generator step-load sequence — the ordered steps in which load is placed on the engine-generator and, for each step, the summed starting kVA, the running kVA carried before the step, the transient voltage dip and the recovery time, by the method of GSB-01.

Company Operations Facility (COF), Building 4410, Fort Calder, Georgia. Prepared by Fort Calder Directorate of Public Works for the using unit. Revision B, 30 June 2026.

4.3 Electrical rooms are conditioned; maximum 85 F.

5.1 Conductors: copper for all feeders and branch circuits.

7 Revision history

IES-26 Rev 4




 IES-26 Fort Calder Installation Electrical Design Standard — Revision 4
 (February 2026)
 Directorate of Public Works, Engineering Division. Applies to all new construction on Fort Calder. Where this standard
 is more stringent than the Unified Facilities Criteria it governs; it never relaxes them.

 1 General

 1.3 No state or local electrical code amendments apply on the installation.

 1.4 Site conditions: inland; no salt-spray or corrosive areas. Cooling design dry bulb (0.4 %) 97 F (36 C); maximum
 recorded ambient 38 C; heating design dry bulb (99.6 %) 18 F (-8 C).

 1.5 The electrical coordination model issued with the contract drawings (50_bim/BLDG4410-E_RevC.ifc) is a contract
 document of equal standing with the drawings. Dimensions, equipment and luminaire locations, luminaire quantities
 and routed raceway lengths are taken from that model; they are not dimensioned or scheduled on the drawings.
 Where the model and a drawing disagree, report the discrepancy to the Contracting Officer before proceeding.

 4 Wiring

 4.1 Copper conductors only. 4.2 Insulation: feeders XHHW-2; branch circuits THHN/THWN-2.

 4.3 Phase identification: 480Y/277 V brown, orange, yellow, neutral gray; 208Y/120 V black, red, blue, neutral white.

 4.4 Metal-clad (MC) and armored (AC) cable are not permitted in new buildings.

 4.5 Raceways: EMT concealed and above ceilings; RMC exposed below 8 ft in mechanical and electrical rooms and
 exposed on building exteriors; PVC Schedule 40 underground and in slabs, with RMC or PVC-coated RMC elbows
 and risers; liquidtight flexible metal conduit for final connections to vibrating equipment, 6 ft maximum. ENT, LFNC
 and surface nonmetallic raceway are not permitted.

 4.6 Raceway fill. Where more than two conductors are installed in one raceway, the sum of the overall cross-sectional
 areas of the conductors must not exceed 40 percent of the interior cross-sectional area of the raceway. Take the
 conductor overall areas from the project conductor data sheet CDS-7 and the raceway interior areas from the project
 raceway data sheet RDS-1; the corresponding tables of NFPA 70 Chapter 9 are not reproduced in this standard and
 are cited by designation only. Install each parallel conductor set of a feeder in its own raceway; a feeder run must not
 carry more parallel sets than it has raceways. Count, in each raceway, three phase conductors, one neutral of the
 same size as the phase conductors, and one equipment grounding conductor. Size the equipment grounding
 conductor of a feeder the same size as the phase conductor where the phase conductor is smaller than 250 kcmil,
 and one size smaller than the phase conductor in the CDS-7 size list where the phase conductor is 250 kcmil or
 larger. Where a phase conductor is increased in size for voltage drop, increase the equipment grounding conductor
 by the same rule.

 4.7 Voltage drop. UFC 3-501-01 paragraph 3-2.7.1 governs and is adopted without change: 3 percent maximum for
 feeders and service conductors, 3 percent maximum for branch circuits, and 5 percent maximum total from the point
 of Government ownership to the furthest outlet. In addition, and more stringently, limit the voltage drop of any feeder
 of the emergency system to 2 percent of nominal voltage. A feeder is a feeder of the emergency system when it
 carries emergency system load, that is: the feeder from the normal source to the emergency system transfer switch;
 the feeder from the alternate (engine-generator) source to that same transfer switch; and every feeder on the load
 side of that transfer switch, including the primary and secondary feeders of any transformer serving emergency
 system load. The emergency system transfer switch is the transfer switch shown on the one-line diagram as serving
 NFPA 70 Article 700 loads. Feeders serving only optional standby (NFPA 70 Article 702) load are not feeders of the
 emergency system and keep the UFC allowance, as do the service conductors, which are not feeders. Calculate



Fort Calder DPW Page 1
 IES-26 Rev 4



 feeder voltage drop over the one-way routed length of the feeder.

 5 Distribution equipment

 5.1 Panelboards: copper bus, door-in-door hinged trim, bolt-on breakers.

 5.2 Surge protective devices: external units mounted adjacent to the protected equipment, 3 ft maximum lead length,
 with surge counter and Form C dry contacts.

 5.4 Nameplates: normal power black letters on white; emergency and standby power white letters on red.

 6 Grounding

 6.1 Building grounding electrode system resistance: 10 ohms maximum, measured by the fall-of-potential method.

 7 Seismic

 7.2 Designated seismic systems: the engine-generator set, the emergency (life-safety) transfer switch and distribution
 (ATS-L, T-E1, LE1) and emergency system raceways. Component importance factor Ip = 1.5 for designated seismic
 systems and 1.0 for other electrical components.

 8 Metering

 8.1 Advanced electric meter at the building main switchboard, Modbus TCP to the installation meter data
 management system (MDMS), 15-minute interval data. No other remote communication from the switchboard. Meter:
 three-phase 4-wire transformer-rated socket meter, Form 9S, ANSI C12.20 accuracy class 0.2, with test switch.
 Detailed ASHRAE 90.1 energy monitoring is not authorized.

 9 Testing

 9.1 Acceptance testing to NETA ATS by an independent NETA-accredited company with a NETA Level III lead
 technician. Scope: switchboard MSB; 480 V panelboards; dry-type transformers; feeders 100 A and larger (insulation
 resistance); grounding electrode system (fall-of-potential); SPDs; ground-fault protection on the main; generator and
 transfer switch (26 32 15 / 26 36 23 field tests witnessed).

 9.2 Power system studies are modelled in SKM PowerTools; deliver the native model files.

 10 Engine-generators and transfer switches

 10.1 Fuel: ultra-low-sulfur No. 2 diesel; biodiesel blends are not permitted. NFPA 110 designation: Class equal to the
 required on-site runtime in hours, Type 10, Level 1 for systems supplying NFPA 70 Article 700 loads.

 10.2 On-site fuel: 72 hours at full load minimum in a UL 142 double-wall sub-base tank with leak detection; the
 installation fuel delivery contract provides the remainder of seven days.

 10.3 Sound: 72 dBA maximum at 23 ft from the enclosure.

 10.4 Emissions: EPA-certified emergency stationary engine (40 CFR 60 Subpart IIII); covered by the installation air
 permit - no project air permit; the Contractor submits the EPA engine certificate to the installation environmental
 office.

 10.5 Field test: 4-hour resistive load bank test at 100 % of the nameplate kW rating.

 10.6 Transfer switches: 4-pole, open transition with in-phase monitor. Separate transfer switches for the emergency
 system (NFPA 70 Article 700) and for optional standby loads; the optional standby switch transfers 30 seconds after



Fort Calder DPW Page 2
 IES-26 Rev 4



 the emergency switch.

 10.7 Generator performance class: ISO 8528 class G2. Engine-generator transient performance is further limited for
 this installation as follows, and these limits are the project's requirement wherever the guide specification asks the
 designer to insert a value. On any load step of the step-load sequence, whether that step is the application or the
 rejection of load: the transient voltage dip must not exceed 15 percent of rated voltage; the set must recover to within
 2 percent of rated voltage within 3 seconds of the step; and the transient frequency deviation must not exceed 5
 percent of rated frequency. These limits are more stringent than the envelope quoted in the guide specification for
 engine-generator sets (which contemplates up to 30 percent voltage deviation and a recovery time of 3 to 5 seconds
 for a set taking full load in one step); the more stringent installation requirement governs. Demonstrate compliance by
 the step-load sequence prepared under the project's generator step-load basis, and verify it at the field test.

 11 Lighting

 11.1 Interior light sources: 4100 K maximum; CRI 80 minimum.

 11.2 Luminaire efficacy (FEMP-designated levels): troffers 120 lm/W, linear ambient 120 lm/W, downlights 90 lm/W,
 exterior area 105 lm/W minimum. Drivers: 0-10 V dimming.

 11.3 Lighting controls: stand-alone localized room controls; no networked or wireless lighting control system; no
 connection to the utility monitoring and control system.

 11.4 Exterior lighting: 3000 K maximum; CRI 70 minimum; parking-lot luminaires B2-U0-G2 maximum, wall packs
 B1-U0-G1; optical compartment IP66; driver surge protection 10 kV/10 kA; ANSI C136.41 7-pin receptacle on

 FDB-01 Feeder Design Basis — Building 4410 (Rev 1)
 Harlan Sato Engineers LLC (A/E, Designer of Record). Establishes the method by which every feeder of Building
 4410 is sized. This memorandum states the method and the input data only; it states no result. The conductor size,
 the number of parallel sets and, where required, the corrected raceway size for each feeder are developed in the
 electrical design basis workbook.

 1. Scope and governing criteria

 Every feeder listed in Table 1 is sized to satisfy all three of the following simultaneously: (a) allowable ampacity not
 less than the design load; (b) voltage drop not more than the allowance of the installation electrical design standard
 IES-26 paragraph 4.7, which adopts UFC 3-501-01 paragraph 3-2.7.1 and tightens the feeders of the emergency
 system; and (c) raceway fill not more than the limit of IES-26 paragraph 4.6. Conductors are copper throughout (OPR
 paragraph 5.1, IES-26 paragraph 4.1), 75 C rated, with 75 C terminations. Conductor properties are from conductor
 data sheet CDS-7; raceway interior areas are from raceway data sheet RDS-1.

 2. Feeder design load and geometry

 The design load of each feeder is given in Table 1. For a feeder to a panelboard it is the connected load of the panel
 schedule on drawing E-701 with the demand factors of the generator and load calculation GLC-01; for a transformer
 primary feeder it is the load corresponding to the nominal output rating of the transformer; for a feeder to a transfer
 switch it is the load transferred by that switch.

 The one-way routed length of each feeder, and the trade size and number of raceways in each feeder run, are NOT
 stated on the drawings. They are taken from the electrical coordination model 50_bim/BLDG4410-E_RevC.ifc, in
 which each raceway run carries the feeder tag of Table 1 as its reference property. Take the one-way routed length
 as the total developed length of the routed raceway run of that feeder, including the vertical rises and drops,
 measured along the centre line of the raceway from the source termination to the load termination. Do not use a
 straight-line distance and do not use the raceways of any other system or of a superseded revision.

 3. Voltage drop

 Calculate the line-to-line voltage drop of a three-phase feeder as

    VD (volts) = sqrt(3) x I x (R x cos(theta) + X x sin(theta)) x L / 1000 / N

 in which I is the design load of Table 1 in amperes; R and X are the alternating-current resistance at 75 C and the
 reactance, in ohms per 1000 feet, of one conductor of the selected size, read from conductor data sheet CDS-7; L is
 the one-way routed length in feet taken from the coordination model as described in paragraph 2; and N is the
 number of parallel conductor sets.

 The design power factor is 0.9 lagging for every feeder, so cos(theta) = 0.9 and sin(theta) = sqrt(1 - 0.9 x 0.9) =
 0.4359. Do not use a different power factor for individual feeders.

 Express the voltage drop as a percentage of the nominal line-to-line voltage of Table 1: VD (per cent) = 100 x VD
 (volts) / V(nominal). Compare that percentage with the allowance of IES-26 paragraph 4.7 for the feeder concerned.
 Each feeder is evaluated over its own length only; the cumulative check against the total allowance is made
 separately in the design basis workbook.

 4. Raceway fill

 Each parallel conductor set occupies one raceway of the feeder run. A feeder run therefore cannot carry more parallel
 sets than it has raceways; a design with more sets than the modelled run has raceways is infeasible and must be
 rejected.

 Each set consists of five conductors: three phase conductors, one full-size neutral of the same size as the phase
 conductors, and one equipment grounding conductor. Size the equipment grounding conductor by the rule of IES-26
 paragraph 4.6: the same size as the phase conductor where the phase conductor is smaller than 250 kcmil, and one
 size smaller than the phase conductor in the CDS-7 size list where the phase conductor is 250 kcmil or larger.

 The area occupied in one raceway is therefore

    A(occupied) = 4 x A(phase conductor) + 1 x A(equipment grounding conductor)

 using the overall areas of column 4 of CDS-7. The percentage fill of that raceway is 100 x A(occupied) / A(interior), in
 which A(interior) is the interior cross-sectional area of the raceway, read from raceway data sheet RDS-1 for the
 raceway material of Table 1 and the trade size shown in the coordination model. The limit is the percentage of IES-26
 paragraph 4.6.




Harlan Sato Engineers LLC (A/E, Designer of Record) Page 2
 FDB-01 Rev 1



 For the feeders routed in the underground duct bank, the conduit fill and the jam ratio are also submittal items under
 Section 33 71 02 paragraph 3.3; the fill computed by this paragraph is the value to be reported.

 5. Ampacity

 The allowable ampacity of the feeder is N x (the 75 C ampacity of one conductor of the selected size, column 5 of
 CDS-7), in which N is the number of parallel sets. The allowable ampacity must not be less than the design load of
 Table 1. Terminations are rated 75 C throughout, so the 75 C column governs at every termination.

 6. The coordination model governs the raceway size

 The raceway trade size shown in the coordination model is the size of the installed raceway and it governs the fill
 calculation. Where no conductor in the CDS-7 catalogue, in any permitted number of parallel sets, can satisfy
 ampacity, voltage drop and raceway fill simultaneously in the raceway the model shows, the model is in error. In that
 case record the discrepancy as a finding against the coordination model and state, as part of the finding, the raceway
 trade size the design requires: the smallest trade size of the same raceway material in which a compliant conductor
 selection exists. Do not silently exceed the fill limit, do not relax the voltage drop allowance, and do not assume a
 raceway size that the model does not show unless the finding is recorded.

 7. Data sources

 Conductor resistance, reactance, overall area and 75 C ampacity: CDS-7. Raceway interior area: RDS-1. Raceway
 material by feeder: Table 1 of this memorandum, which follows IES-26 paragraph 4.5. Routed length, raceway trade
 size and number of raceways per run: the coordination model 50_bim/BLDG4410-E_RevC.ifc. Design load: Table 1
 of this memorandum, from E-701 and GLC-01. Voltage drop allowances: IES-26 paragraph 4.7 and UFC 3-501-01
 paragraph 3-2.7.1. Raceway fill limit and equipment grounding conductor sizing: IES-26 paragraph 4.6.

 SCB-01 Short-Circuit Study Basis — Building 4410 (Rev 1)
 Harlan Sato Engineers LLC (A/E, Designer of Record). Prepared for the 35 % design submittal; to be updated for

 1. Purpose

 Establish the method and data used to determine the available short-circuit current at each bus, which sets the
 minimum short-circuit current ratings stated in the project specifications.

 2. Method

 Per-unit impedance method, three-phase bolted fault, 1.0 per-unit prefault voltage, complex impedances (R + jX).

 Specify for each bus the next standard short-circuit current rating at or above the calculated total. Standard ratings

=================== 40_studies/PCB-01_Photometric_Calculation_Basis_Rev1.pdf
PCB-01 Rev 1




 PCB-01 Photometric Calculation Basis — Building 4410 (Rev 1)
 Harlan Sato Engineers LLC (A/E, Designer of Record). Establishes the method by which the interior illuminance of
 every space of Building 4410 is calculated and by which a luminaire quantity is verified. This memorandum states the
 method and the input data only; it states no calculated illuminance, uniformity, lighting power density or luminaire
 quantity.

 1. Governing criteria

 Section 26 51 00 requires computer-generated photometric plans for each space, using the applicable light loss
 factor, to verify that the proposed luminaires and locations meet the required performance criteria. That section
 establishes, for the calculation: horizontal illuminance taken at a maximum of every one foot (305 mm) across the
 task area; a recommended light loss factor of 0.81 for LED luminaires; uniformity calculated as the ratio of the
 average calculated illuminance over the minimum calculated illuminance of the calculation grid; and a 10 percent
 margin of error on each target, a 'Minimum Average' being an average taken over the entire task area that may not be
 less than the stated value within that margin.

 The target illumination levels for each interior application, in the 'Minimum Average' and 'Uniformity' vocabulary of that
 section, are given in the installation electrical design standard IES-26 paragraph 11.6. The whole-building interior
 lighting power density limit is IES-26 paragraph 11.7. Surface reflectances are scheduled on A-601. Room
 dimensions, ceiling heights, luminaire positions and luminaire quantities are taken from the electrical coordination
 model 50_bim/BLDG4410-E_RevC.ifc.

 The light loss factor used for every LED luminaire in this project is 0.81. The margin of error applied to each target is
 10 percent: a calculated average maintained illuminance is acceptable when it is not less than 0.9 times the Minimum
 Average of IES-26 paragraph 11.6, and a calculated uniformity is acceptable when it is not more than 1.1 times the
 Uniformity limit of that paragraph.

 2. Luminous flux of a luminaire: zonal integration of the candela table

 Each interior luminaire type is described by an LM-63 photometric file named in the luminaire schedule E-501 and
 issued in 40_product_data/photometrics/. The candela table of that file gives, for each horizontal angle present in the
 file, the luminous intensity in candelas at the vertical angles 0 to 90 degrees from nadir in 5 degree steps.

 The luminous flux of the luminaire to be used in this calculation is the flux obtained by integrating that candela table. It
 is NOT the rated lamp lumens written in the file header and it is NOT the rated lamp lumens scheduled on E-501;
 those are lamp values and are larger than the flux the luminaire emits. Obtain the flux as follows.

 a. For each vertical angle in the table, form the mean intensity over the horizontal angles. Where the file contains a
 single horizontal plane, the mean is that plane's value at that vertical angle. Where the file contains more than one
 horizontal plane, take the trapezoidal average over the horizontal angles present: sum, over each adjacent pair of
 horizontal angles a and b, the quantity (I(a) + I(b)) / 2 multiplied by (b - a); then divide that sum by (the last horizontal
 angle minus the first horizontal angle). The files are quadrant symmetric and carry horizontal angles from 0 to 90
 degrees.

 b. Sum the zonal contributions over the vertical angles. For each adjacent pair of vertical angles t1 and t2, add

    2 x pi x (cos t1 - cos t2) x (Ibar(t1) + Ibar(t2)) / 2

 in which Ibar is the mean intensity of step (a) at that vertical angle and the angles are in radians. The sum over all
 adjacent pairs is the luminous flux of one luminaire, in lumens.

 3. Intensity at an arbitrary direction: bilinear interpolation



Harlan Sato Engineers LLC (A/E, Designer of Record) Page 1
 PCB-01 Rev 1



 The intensity at a vertical angle theta from nadir and a horizontal angle phi is interpolated bilinearly from the candela
 table. Fold the horizontal angle into the range 0 to 90 degrees by quadrant symmetry: take the absolute value, reduce
 modulo 180 degrees and, if the result exceeds 90 degrees, replace it by 180 degrees minus the result. Interpolate
 linearly between the two bounding horizontal planes of the file, and linearly between the two bounding vertical angles
 of the table (the vertical angles are evenly spaced, so the fraction is the remainder of theta divided by the step,
 divided by the step). Where the file contains a single horizontal plane, no horizontal interpolation is made. The
 intensity is zero at and above 90 degrees from nadir.

 4. Calculation grid and work plane

 The work plane is a horizontal plane 2.5 feet above the finished floor of the space. The calculation grid covers the
 whole floor area of the space, which is the task area for these targets.

 Grid points are spaced 1 foot apart on each horizontal axis, and the first point on each axis is 0.5 foot from the wall.
 On an axis of extent E feet the number of points is therefore floor((E - 2 x 0.5) / 1) + 1, not less than one, and the
 points lie at the room origin on that axis plus 0.5 plus 1 times 0, 1, 2 and so on. The grid is the full cross product of the
 points of the two axes. Take the room extents and the room origin from the coordination model.

 5. Direct component

 Let h be the mounting height of the luminaires above the work plane: the height of the luminaire above the finished
 floor of its storey, taken directly from the placement of the luminaire in the coordination model, less the work plane
 height of paragraph 4. All luminaires of one space are at the same height. Where h is not positive the space cannot
 be calculated by this method.

 For each grid point, sum over every luminaire in the space the quantity

    I(theta, phi) x (h / d) / (d x d)

 in which, writing dx and dy for the horizontal offsets from the luminaire to the grid point: d = sqrt(dx x dx + dy x dy + h
 x h) is the slant distance; theta = atan(sqrt(dx x dx + dy x dy) / h) is the vertical angle from nadir; and phi = atan(|dy| /
 |dx|) is the horizontal angle, measured from the long axis of the luminaire, which is the +X axis of the coordination
 model for every modelled interior luminaire. Where the grid point is directly under the luminaire take phi as zero;
 where dx is zero and dy is not, take phi as 90 degrees. The factor (h / d) is the cosine of the angle of incidence, so the
 expression is the inverse-square-cosine illuminance in footcandles when I is in candelas and the distances are in feet.

 Multiply the sum at each grid point by the light loss factor 0.81 to obtain the direct component of the maintained
 illuminance at that point. The average direct component is the arithmetic mean of the direct component over all grid
 points.

 6. Interreflected component

 The interreflected component is uniform over the space and is obtained from the flux that does not reach the work
 plane directly, redistributed by the average reflectance of the room surfaces:

    E(indirect) = rho / (1 - rho) x (PHI x LLF - E(direct, average) x A(work plane)) / A(room)

 in which PHI is the luminous flux of one luminaire from paragraph 2 multiplied by the number of luminaires in the
 space; LLF is 0.81; E(direct, average) is the average direct component of paragraph 5; A(work plane) is the floor area
 of the space; and A(room) is the total area of the room surfaces, taken as

    A(room) = 2 x A(floor) + 2 x H x (W + D)

 with W and D the room extents and H the finished ceiling height, all from the coordination model. The term in brackets
 is taken as zero if it would be negative.



Harlan Sato Engineers LLC (A/E, Designer of Record) Page 2
 PCB-01 Rev 1



 rho is the area-weighted average reflectance of the room surfaces,

    rho = (rho(ceiling) x A(floor) + rho(floor) x A(floor) + rho(wall) x 2 x H x (W + D)) / A(room)

 using the ceiling, wall and floor reflectances scheduled for that room on A-601.

 7. Reported quantities

 The average maintained illuminance of the space is the average direct component plus the interreflected component.
 The minimum maintained illuminance is the smallest direct component over the grid plus the interreflected
 component. The uniformity is the average maintained illuminance divided by the minimum maintained illuminance.
 The lighting power density of the space is the number of luminaires multiplied by the scheduled input watts of the
 type, divided by the floor area of the space. The whole-building interior lighting power density is the total input watts of
 all interior luminaires of the building divided by the total interior floor area of all spaces, and is compared with the limit
 of IES-26 paragraph 11.7.

 8. Re-layout where a quantity is revised

 Where the calculation confirms the luminaire quantity shown in the coordination model, the luminaire positions of the
 model govern and are used as they are.

 Where a different quantity n is evaluated for a space, do not attempt to preserve the modelled positions: lay the n
 luminaires out again on a uniform grid over the whole space, by the following rule. Take the number of columns
 (along the X axis of the space) as the nearest whole number to sqrt(n x W / D), not less than one and not more than
 n, in which W and D are the room extents along X and Y. Take the number of rows as n divided by the number of
 columns, rounded up to a whole number. Place the luminaires at the centres of the cells of that row-by-column grid:
 the luminaire in row r and column c, counting r and c from zero, is at

    x = X(origin) + W x (c + 0.5) / columns, y = Y(origin) + D x (r + 0.5) / rows

 filling row by row, and keep the first n positions so generated. The mounting height is unchanged. This rule is used for
 every space and every quantity so that two engineers evaluating the same quantity obtain the same layout.

 9. Data sources

 Candela tables: the LM-63 file named for each type on E-501. Input watts, type marks and descriptions: E-501.
 Surface reflectances: A-601. Room extents, ceiling heights, luminaire quantities, luminaire positions and luminaire
 mounting heights: the coordination model 50_bim/BLDG4410-E_RevC.ifc. Illuminance targets and uniformity limits:
 IES-26 paragraph 11.6. Lighting power density limit: IES-26 paragraph 11.7. Light loss factor, grid spacing, uniformity
 definition and margin of error: Section 26 51 00 and this memorandum.




Harlan Sato Engineers LLC (A/E, Designer of Record) Page 3
 =================== 40_studies/GSB-01_Generator_Step-Load_Basis_Rev1.pdf
GSB-01 Rev 1




 GSB-01 Generator Step-Load Basis — Building 4410 (Rev 1)
 Harlan Sato Engineers LLC (A/E, Designer of Record). Establishes the method by which the sequence in which load
 is placed on the standby engine-generator GEN-1 is developed and verified. This memorandum states the method
 and the input data only; it states no transient voltage dip, no recovery time and no step sequence.

 1. Scope

 On loss of the normal source the engine-generator starts and the transfer switches transfer their loads to it. The load
 is not placed on the set all at once: it is placed in steps. The step-load sequence is a design deliverable. Each step is
 a group of load tags placed on the set at the same instant; the steps are taken in order, the set recovering to steady
 state between steps.

 2. Load data

 The loads that transfer to the engine-generator, the running kVA and the starting (locked-rotor) kVA of each, and the
 transfer switch that serves each, are scheduled on the mechanical equipment schedule M-601 (sheet 'Generator
 transfer loads') and, for the motor-driven equipment, in the nameplate data of sheet 'M-601'. Machine data for the set
 are on the manufacturer's data sheet GEN-1. Acceptance limits are in the installation electrical design standard
 IES-26 paragraph 10.7.

 3. Transient voltage dip of a step

 Calculate the transient voltage dip caused by one step as

    dip (per cent) = 100 x Xd2 x kVA(step) / ( kVA(alternator) + Xd2 x ( kVA(step) + kVA(running) ) )

 in which Xd2 is the saturated direct-axis subtransient reactance of the alternator in per unit on its own kVA base, from
 data sheet GEN-1 (0.12 per unit); kVA(alternator) is the standby kVA rating of the set from data sheet GEN-1 (187.5
 kVA); kVA(step) is the sum of the starting (locked-rotor) kVA of every load tag added at that step; and kVA(running) is
 the sum of the running kVA of every load tag already carried by the set immediately before that step. For the first step
 kVA(running) is zero.

 A load that is not motor-driven has a starting kVA equal to its running kVA, as scheduled. Use the scheduled
 locked-rotor kVA as it is; do not apply a starting-current multiplier of your own and do not apply a reduced-voltage
 starting credit, since no unit is scheduled with a reduced-voltage starter.

 4. Recovery time of a step

 Take the time for the set to recover from a step as

    t(recovery, seconds) = 0.6 + 0.08 x dip (per cent)

 using the dip of paragraph 3 for that step, expressed in per cent. The recovery time of every step must satisfy the limit
 of IES-26 paragraph 10.7.

 5. Rules the sequence must satisfy

 a. Every load that transfers to the engine-generator must appear in the sequence exactly once. A load may not be
 started twice and no load may be omitted.

 b. Every load of the emergency system, that is every load served by the emergency (life safety) transfer switch, which
 is the transfer switch identified on E-601 as serving NFPA 70 Article 700 loads, must be carried by the first step. The
 emergency transfer switch restores its loads within 10 seconds of loss of the normal source (IES-26 paragraph 10.6),



Harlan Sato Engineers LLC (A/E, Designer of Record) Page 1
 GSB-01 Rev 1



 so its loads cannot wait for a later step. Optional standby loads may be placed on any step.

 c. The transient voltage dip of every step must not exceed the limit of IES-26 paragraph 10.7.

 d. The total running load carried by the set when every load has transferred, taken as the sum of the running kVA of
 all transferred loads multiplied by the rated power factor of the set from data sheet GEN-1 (0.8), must not exceed the
 standby kilowatt rating of the set (150 kW).

 e. A step may not be empty.

 6. Deliverable

 State the sequence as an ordered list of steps, each step being the list of load tags of M-601 placed on the set at that

Cordell Lighting Group - photometric file set for Building 4410
Issued 2026-04-17 by Vantia Photometric Laboratory.

Format
  Every file in this folder is an ANSI/IESNA LM-63-2002 photometric data file: plain ASCII, CRLF
  line endings, the identifier line IESNA:LM-63-2002, the required keyword block, and TILT=NONE.
  Photometric type 1 (Type C) with luminous opening dimensions in metres (units type 2). Vertical
  angles run 0 to 90 degrees in 5 degree steps; the candela rows are written one row per horizontal
  angle, each row holding one value for every vertical angle.

Basis of the numbers
  These are relative photometry files. The lumens-per-lamp field of the first data line is the RATED
  lamp lumens of the light engine, taken from the lamp data, not the measured output of the
  luminaire. The candela values are reported per those rated lamp lumens and already carry the
  luminaire efficiency, so the candela table integrates to less than the rated lamp lumens. The
  candela multiplier and the ballast factor are both 1.000 and have been applied to the tabulated
  values; no further multiplier is needed. Total luminaire lumens are not a field of the format -
  obtain them by integrating the candela table over solid angle (zonal lumen summation).
  Input watts on the second data line is the measured luminaire input power and is not adjusted by
  the ballast factor.

Files
  L1.ies   2 ft by 4 ft recessed LED troffer                30.0 W   CLG-TR24-40L-35K-UNV
  L2.ies   2 ft by 2 ft recessed LED troffer                21.0 W   CLG-TR22-28L-35K-UNV

  L4.ies   6 in recessed LED downlight                      14.0 W   CLG-DL6-15L-35K-UNV

  W1.ies   LED wall pack, full cutoff                       25.0 W   CLG-WP30-30L-30K-UNV
  P1.ies   LED area luminaire, pole mounted, asymmetric    100.0 W   CLG-AL4-120L-30K-UNV

  asymmetric, bilaterally symmetric about the 0-180 degree photometric plane, and full cutoff (no
  output at or above 90 degrees from nadir).

import json, collections, re
rows=json.load(open('/filesystem/work/segs.json'))
runs=collections.OrderedDict()
for r in rows:
    m=re.match(r'CND-(.+)-(\d+)-(\d+)$', r['name'])
    feeder, run, seg = m.group(1), int(m.group(2)), int(m.group(3))
    runs.setdefault((r['ref'],run),[]).append(r)
for (ref,run),segs in runs.items():
    segs.sort(key=lambda r:int(r['name'].split('-')[-1]))
    L=sum(s['L_mm'] for s in segs)
    # continuity
    gaps=[]
    for a,b in zip(segs[:-1],segs[1:]):
        pa=a['pts'][0][-1]; pb=b['pts'][0][0]
        d=sum((x-y)**2 for x,y in zip(pa,pb))**0.5
        if d>1: gaps.append((a['name'],b['name'],round(d,1)))
    print(ref, run, len(segs), 'L=%.1f mm = %.2f ft'%(L, L/304.8), segs[0]['nd'], 'start',segs[0]['pts'][0][0],'end',segs[-1]['pts'][0][-1], 'gaps',gaps)
EOF

3-2.7         Voltage Drop.

The following voltage drop requirements apply to AC and DC constant voltage systems
1000V or less unless more stringent criteria apply. The following does not apply to
constant current systems or distribution systems over 1000V. In situations where the
voltage within a facility’s distribution system is increased over this threshold, the voltage
drop requirements shall restart assuming nominal voltage when transformed below the
threshold.

400Hz systems must be designed for voltage drop in accordance with UFC 3-555-01N
requirements.

If the phase conductor size is increased for voltage drop, increase the size of the
equipment grounding conductor proportional to the circular mil increase of the phase
conductor in accordance with NFPA 70 Section 250.122.

              Permitted Voltage Drop.

The maximum voltage drop permitted must not exceed 5%. Unless stricter
requirements apply as adopted by this or other UFCs, feeders and service conductors
must be limited to 3% voltage drop and branch circuits must be limited to 3% voltage
drop, with no greater than 5% total. The starting point for this calculation is defined
below.

Calculation limits must be based on the cumulative amount of voltage drop seen at a
given location in the distribution system from the start of calculation identified below, not
on an individual basis by circuit.




                                             24
                                                                            UFC 3-501-01
                                                                      27 November 2024


             General Voltage Drop Mitigation Strategies and Impacts.

Voltage drop can be mitigated through various strategies, including increasing
conductor size, reducing the circuit’s load, decreasing the conductor’s length,
decreasing conductor temperature, and improving power factor. When establishing
distribution equipment placement within a facility, locate panelboards relatively central
to the loads supplied to minimize circuit lengths. Likewise, routing the majority of the
distribution at 480/277V and stepping down to 208/120V more locally to the loads
served will yield a lower voltage drop to the end devices; this strategy needs to evaluate
a balance between transformer and circuit costs, as well as requirements to submeter
different load types when applicable.

Note increased conductor sizes will yield lower conductor resistances, lead to increased
fault current values, and impact arc flash values at the equipment buses, potentially
leading to protection coordination issues. Designers must ensure all conductor sizes
are established prior to performing final fault current and arc flash calculations, and
update safety calculations when modifying existing systems.

             Voltage Drop Relationship with Utilization Voltage.

Voltage drop calculations focus on energy loss through conductors, and voltage drop
contributes to utilization voltage for end users. However, voltage drop and utilization
voltage, which is the actual voltage seen at end-use devices and equipment, are not
synonymous. Devices and equipment have acceptable utilization voltage ranges within
which operation can occur, the lower bound of which can be of a lower voltage than
yielded by the maximum permitted voltage drop alone. Other system losses occur
throughout the distribution system, most notably through transformers, and the voltage
delivered by the utility service may deviate from the nominal voltage assumed in
calculations. Transformer tap settings aid in providing appropriate downstream
utilization voltage, however, the use of transformer taps does not negate energy losses
incurred through conductor impedance voltage drop.

Design and construction personnel must remain cognizant of the utilization voltage
requirements for the equipment and appliances served. Adjustments to the distribution
system, such as the use of transformer taps and/or an increase in conductor sizes, must
be performed accordingly to ensure proper utilization voltage is provided to the end use
devices while simultaneously satisfying the voltage drop energy conservation
requirements.

Practices used to boost utilization voltage at the load must not be used as a method to
comply with voltage drop requirements.

             Calculation Assumptions and Procedures.

3-2.7.4.1    Initial Voltage.

The use of service transformer taps must not be assumed to compensate for voltage
drop on the service-entrance equipment side of the calculation start point. Calculations
                                           25
                                                                             UFC 3-501-01
                                                                       27 November 2024


must assume the nominal system voltage (i.e., 208V, 240V, 480V) is present at the
location described for the calculation starting point.

3-2.7.4.2     Starting Point.

Voltage drop calculations must start at the point of government ownership (i.e.,
transformer, disconnect switch, meter cabinet, or similar). Where the government owns
the exterior distribution upstream of the service transformer, the calculation must start at
the service transformer secondary lugs. Where the facility is without a service
transformer and supplied by independent generator or energy storage system, the
calculation must start at such power supply’s output terminals.

3-2.7.4.3     Load Estimations.

3-2.7.4.3.1   Capacity.

The capacity must be 100% of a circuit breaker or fuse device’s nominal rating (e.g.,
100A standard (80%) devices and 100A continuous (100%) devices are both
considered 100A capacity) for voltage drop calculation purposes. See UFC 3-520-01
regarding Adjustable-Trip Devices.

3-2.7.4.3.2   Feeder Loads.

Size feeders to accommodate the maximum permitted load based on the circuit
ampacity. Exceptions to this are as follows:

       a.     Transformer Feeders. Per ANSI C57.96, transformers complying with
              the ANSI standard are designed for continuous operation at the specified
              temperature rise for normal life expectancy at the rated kVA. The rated
              kVA may be different than the nameplate or nominal kVA value based
              upon insulation temperature rating, ambient temperature, altitude, and
              other operating conditions.
              For voltage drop purposes, a transformer’s secondary feeders must
              assume a load equivalent to the transformer’s nominal output rating.

              For voltage drop purposes, a transformer’s primary feeders must assume
              the same load as identified above for the secondary feeders PLUS 6%
              transformer loss load.

       b.     Motor Feeders. Motor overcurrent protection is located at the overloads
              and NFPA 70 categorizes the circuits from the circuit breakers to the
              overcurrent protection as feeders. As on transformer primary circuits,
              circuit breakers are sized to account for inrush. Utilize the circuit’s total
              full-load amps (FLA) based on NFPA 70 Article 430 tables for voltage drop
              calculations. Additionally, this circuit must be considered a “branch circuit”
              for voltage drop compliance purposes only.


                                            26
                                                                            UFC 3-501-01
                                                                      27 November 2024


              Fire pumps must comply with the voltage drop requirements identified in
              NFPA 70 Article 695 in lieu of the limits stated in this section.

      c.      Air-Conditioning and Refrigerating Equipment Feeders. The voltage
              drop load must be the rated-load current or full-load current marked on the
              nameplate as identified in NFPA 70 Article 440. Additionally, this circuit
              must be considered a “branch circuit” for voltage drop compliance
              purposes only.
      d.      Variable Frequency Drives/Adjustable Speed Drive Feeders. Feeders
              to variable frequency drives, adjustable speed drives, and similar must be
              sized for voltage drop based on the drive’s maximum input current,
              including any drive losses. Additionally, this circuit must be considered a
              “branch circuit” for voltage drop compliance purposes only.
      e.      Other Feeders Directly Supplying Motor-Based Equipment. Where
              NFPA 70 categorizes conductors as feeders, but the conductors supply
              dedicated motor-based equipment or equipment assemblies such as
              cranes and elevators, the voltage drop calculation load must be the total
              FLA. Application-specific NFPA 70 demand factors may be applied to the
              loads when used for voltage drop calculations. Additionally, this circuit
              must be considered a “branch circuit” for voltage drop compliance
              purposes only.
3-2.7.4.3.3   Branch Circuit Loads.

      a.      Lighting Circuits. Lighting circuits must utilize the total full load of all
              luminaire and non-luminaire devices connected. Where the lighting circuit
              contains non-luminaire components such as room controllers or power
              packs, ensure such loads are captured.
      b.      Receptacle Circuits. Receptacle circuits (including circuits where a
              dedicated receptacle is provided for a single device, appliance, or
              equipment) must use 80% of the circuit’s capacity for voltage drop
              calculations.
      c.      Systems Furniture Circuits. Systems furniture circuits must use 80% of
              the circuit’s capacity for voltage drop calculations.
      d.      Hard-Wired Appliance and Other Non-Receptacle Circuits. Hard-
              wired appliance and other non-receptacle circuits must utilize the total
              connected load on the circuit for voltage drop calculations.

3-2.7.4.4     Circuit Lengths.

3-2.7.4.4.1   Methods.

See UFC 3-520-01 for routing estimation instructions, and utilize the applicable method
as described and assigned below.


                                            27
                                                                             UFC 3-501-01
                                                                       27 November 2024


       a.     End-of-Line Method. Loads on circuits must be at the end of the circuit
              for voltage drop calculations unless otherwise indicated below.
       b.     Point-to-Point Method. Calculate the load contributions to voltage drop
              as a function of the load experienced for a given portion of the circuit
              except as identified in the subsequent entries of this section. That is, the
              entire load on the circuit is experienced to the first device, be it a load,
              splicing/junction point, etc. Beyond that point, the load is diminished for
              the next series or parallel lengths, and only those loads contribute to the
              voltage dropped in the associated circuit length.
              The totality of the voltage dropped on any given path must be evaluated in
              determining a satisfactory conductor size (i.e., the path to one end device
              may experience less voltage drop than the path to a different end device),
              and the more severe condition in a comparison of multiple paths must be
              used for the entire circuit size.

                              CHAPTER 1 INTRODUCTION

1-1           PURPOSE AND SCOPE.

This Unified Facilities Criteria (UFC) has been issued to provide guidance for the design
of interior electrical systems. The criteria contained herein are intended to ensure
economical, durable, efficient, and reliable systems and installations. Whenever unique
conditions and problems are not specifically covered by this UFC, use the applicable
referenced industry standards and other documents for design guidance.

UFC 3-501-01 provides the governing criteria for electrical systems, explains the
delineation between the different electrical-related UFCs, and refers to UFC 3-520-01
for interior electrical system requirements. Modernization of electrical systems within
existing facilities solely for the purpose of meeting design criteria in this UFC is not
required. Upgrades or modifications of existing facilities must apply the design criteria
in this UFC, but it is not intended that an entire facility require modernization solely
because of a minor modification to a part of the facility.

1-2           REISSUES AND CANCELS.

This UFC reissues and cancels UFC 3-520-01, dated 06 October 2015.

1-3           APPLICABILITY.

This UFC applies to planning, design, construction, sustainment, restoration, and
modernization of DoD-owned facilities. It applies to all methods of project delivery and
levels of construction as defined by UFC 1-200-01, Section 1-3.

1-3.1         UFC Scope.

Compliance with this UFC is mandatory for the design of interior electrical systems at all
facilities and bases. This UFC typically applies up to 5 feet beyond the facility envelope.
It also applies to:

        •     Service(s) supplying power from the utility system utilization transformer to
              the wiring system of the facility.
        •     Circuits originating from within the facility that extend beyond the facility
              envelope.
        •     Wiring and connections for supplemental grounding systems.
        •     Wiring from and connections to non-utility equipment supplying power to
              the wiring system of the facility, including engine-generator sets,
              photovoltaic power systems and fuel cells.

Refer to UFC 3-550-01 for exterior electrical systems.



                                              1
                                                                            UFC 3-520-01
                                                                        16 January 2025
                                                              Change 1, 21 January 2026

1-3.2         Host Nation Standards.

In addition to NFPA 70 requirements, facilities located outside of the United States must
also comply with the applicable host nation standards. Host nation voltage and
frequency as defined in UFC 3-510-01 generally applies. Different wiring and grounding
conventions usually apply in other host nations; however, follow the design principles
provided in this UFC to the extent practical.

1-4           GENERAL BUILDING REQUIREMENTS.

Comply with UFC 1-200-01, DoD Building Code. UFC 1-200-01 provides applicability of
model building codes and government unique criteria for typical design disciplines and
building systems, as well as for accessibility, antiterrorism, security, high performance
and sustainability requirements, and safety. Use this UFC in addition to UFC 1-200-01
and the UFCs and government criteria referenced therein.

1-5           CYBERSECURITY.

All facility-related control systems (including systems separate from a utility monitoring
and control system) must be planned, designed, acquired, executed, and maintained in
accordance with UFC 4-010-06, and as required by individual Service Implementation
Policy.

Cybersecurity is implemented to mitigate vulnerabilities to all DoD real property facility-
related control systems to a level that is acceptable to the System Owner and
Authorizing Official. UFC 4-010-06 provides requirements for integrating cybersecurity
into the design and construction of control systems.

1-6           DESIGN STANDARDS.

Comply with the requirements of National Fire Protection Association (NFPA) 70,
National Electrical Code, and the requirements herein. Electrical safety requirements,
including the types of energized work permitted, approval process for energized work,
and Personal Protective Equipment (PPE), applicable to the design, installation, and
operation of electrical systems are provided in UFC 3-560-01.

Note: When a project, or portion of a project, has been designated as requiring Critical
Operations Power Systems (COPS) treatment as a Designated Critical Operations Area
(DCOA) per NFPA 70 Article 708, those requirements identified in the Unified Facility
Criteria that are more stringent than NFPA 70 requirements take precedence over
NFPA requirements. This UFC does not address COPS requirements.

1-7           GLOSSARY.

of the code or standard is not included in this document. Unless otherwise specified,
the most recent edition of the referenced publication applies.

References applicable to a specific topic are also listed and described in the appropriate
sections of this UFC. Codes and standards are referenced throughout this UFC.
Follow the guidance provided in UFC 1-200-01, Section 1-3.1 to establish the

                 CHAPTER 2 GENERAL POWER SYSTEM CRITERIA

2-1           VOLTAGE.

Refer to UFC 3-550-01 for voltage criteria associated with the primary distribution
supply voltage.

Unless there are specialty voltage requirements, base the facility system voltage on the
interior load requirements as follows:

       •      Apply 240/120V for facilities with only single-phase loads.
       •      Apply three-phase, four-wire, 208Y/120V systems for lighting and power
              demand loads less than 150 kVA.
       •      Apply three-phase, four-wire, 480Y/277V systems for lighting and power
              demand loads greater than 150 kVA unless 208Y/120V systems are
              shown to be more cost-effective. Use step-down transformers inside the
              facility as required to obtain lower voltages.
       •      For facilities with demand loads less than or equal to 150 kVA in which
              potential voltage drop issues have been identified, evaluate the life cycle
              cost effectiveness of installing larger conductor sizes and/or buck-boost
              transformers on a 208Y/120V system against the use of a 480Y/277V
              service utilizing step-down transformers. If determined that the life cycle
              cost is effective, the use of a 480Y/277V service shall be used in lieu of a
              208Y/120V service.
2-2           FREQUENCY.

Apply a frequency of 60 Hz for distribution and utilization power.

In locations in which the commercially supplied frequency is other than 60 Hz, such as
50 Hz, use the available supplied frequency to the extent practical. Where frequencies
other than that locally available are required for technical purposes, frequency
conversion or generation equipment can be installed. The facility user will normally
provide this equipment.

                                          16 January 2025
                                Change 1, 21 January 2026
